questions.stem: A nucleophile is defined as

options.text: An electron-rich species able to give away a pair of electrons
options.explanation: Attraction to positive centres follows from that richness.
That is the electrophile.

options.text: Any species with a full negative charge
options.explanation: Definition runs on electron-pair donation, not charge alone.
Nucleophiles are consumed as reactants.

questions.stem: Which conditions convert a halogenoalkane to an alcohol?

options.explanation: That reagent belongs to halide tests, not alcohol synthesis.
Aqueous OH- with gentle warming hydrolyses the C-X bond to the alcohol.
Ethanolic conditions eliminate to the alkene instead.
Ammonia gives amines, and only under ethanolic pressure-heating.

questions.stem: Why must water be the primary solvent for the alcohol route?

options.explanation: Water is the solvent medium, not a catalyst.

options.text: The alcohol dissolves only in water
options.explanation: Solubility of the product is not the governing reason.

options.text: Ethanolic conditions steer the reaction to elimination, forming an alkene
options.explanation: Solvent choice selects the pathway: aqueous substitution versus ethanolic elimination.
No freezing effect is involved.

questions.stem: The hydroxide ion beats water as a nucleophile because

options.text: It is lighter and moves faster
options.explanation: Mass is not the deciding factor.

options.text: It is larger and more visible
options.explanation: Size and visibility are irrelevant.

options.text: Water is not a nucleophile at all
options.explanation: Water is a weak nucleophile - it eventually substitutes.

options.text: It carries a full negative charge where water's oxygen carries only partial charge
options.explanation: Full charge means stronger electron-pair donation and faster attack.

questions.stem: Rank the halogenoalkanes by rate of hydrolysis with aqueous OH-:

options.text: Iodoalkane fastest, then bromo, then chloro, fluoro unreactive
options.explanation: Weakest C-X bond (C-I) breaks fastest; C-F is too strong to react.
Electronegativity is outweighed by bond enthalpy.

options.text: Chloro fastest, since C-Cl is most polar
options.explanation: Polarity suggests but bond strength decides.

options.text: All equal rates, as each carries one halogen
options.explanation: The C-X bond strength varies hugely down the group.

questions.stem: Define the term nucleophile.
questions.modelAnswer: A species rich in electrons that gives a pair away to an electron-deficient centre.

questions.stem: State the conditions and product for the alcohol route.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm aqueous NaOH or KOH (ethanol as co-solvent) gives the alcohol by hydrolysis.

questions.stem: Explain why fluoroalkanes do not undergo the hydroxide substitution at all.
questions.modelAnswer: The C-F bond is the strongest carbon-halogen bond, so hydroxide cannot break it under these conditions.

questions.stem: A chemist accidentally uses pure ethanol as solvent with NaOH instead of aqueous alkali. Predict the organic product and name the reaction class.
questions.modelAnswer: An alkene forms by elimination rather than the intended alcohol; the reaction class switches from nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis) to elimination.

questions.stem: The nucleophile in the nitrile-forming reaction is

options.explanation: The halide departs; it does not attack.
Cyanide donates its carbon lone pair to the halogenoalkane.
Hydroxide gives alcohols, not nitriles.
Ammonia gives amines.

questions.stem: The conditions for forming a nitrile are

options.explanation: That combination gives elimination to the alkene.
Ammonia's route gives primary amines.
Reflux heat with ethanolic cyanide drives the substitution.
The standard route specifies ethanol and reflux.

questions.stem: Bromoethane reacting with ethanolic KCN gives propanenitrile because

options.text: The bromine is replaced by three carbons
options.explanation: Only one carbon is added per substitution.
No dimerisation occurs.

options.text: The ethanol solvent adds a carbon
options.explanation: The solvent does not enter the product.

options.text: The cyanide ion contributes its own carbon, extending the chain from two to three
options.explanation: C2 substrate plus the C of CN- gives a C3 nitrile.

questions.stem: A chemist wants a compound with one more carbon than the best available starting material. The useful reaction is

options.text: Halogenoalkane with ethanolic KCN under reflux
options.explanation: Cyanide substitution adds exactly one carbon.
That route keeps the carbon count unchanged.
Amines also keep the substrate's carbon count.
Water's slow hydrolysis adds no carbon.

questions.stem: In propanenitrile formed from bromoethane, the nitrile carbon counts as

options.explanation: The nitrile carbon carries the highest priority and is numbered 1.
Nitrile carbon is included in the parent count.

options.text: A side group outside the chain count
options.explanation: The -C#N carbon is part of the counted chain.
It is the very carbon cyanide donated.

questions.stem: State the product class and conditions for the cyanide route.
questions.modelAnswer: A nitrile forms when the halogenoalkane is heated under reflux with ethanolic KCN.

questions.stem: State the synthetic value of the cyanide substitution.
questions.modelAnswer: It extends the carbon chain by one carbon, enabling synthesis of larger molecules from smaller starting materials.

questions.stem: Explain why the cyanide ion is nucleophilic.
questions.modelAnswer: Cyanide carries a full negative charge with a lone pair on its carbon, so it donates an electron pair into the halogenoalkane's electron-poor carbon.

questions.stem: Predict the organic product of 1-chloropropane with ethanolic KCN under reflux, and give its carbon count.
questions.modelAnswer: Butanenitrile: the C3 chain gains cyanide's carbon to give a four-carbon nitrile (the nitrile carbon counted as C1).

questions.stem: The nucleophile in primary amine synthesis is

options.explanation: NH4+ has no lone pair to donate.
The halide leaves; it does not attack.
Ammonia's lone pair performs the substitution.
The route uses ammonia molecules.

questions.stem: Excess ammonia is used because

options.text: Ammonia is expensive and must be recovered
options.explanation: Excess implies using more, not saving.
Pressure is applied regardless.
No neutralisation role is assigned to excess NH3.

options.text: The amine product is more reactive than ammonia and could undergo further substitution
options.explanation: Flooding with NH3 keeps collisions on ammonia rather than the amine.

questions.stem: Bromoethane with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure and heat gives

options.explanation: NH2 replaces Br on the two-carbon chain.
That is the cyanide route's product.
Further substitution is suppressed by the excess ammonia.
That is the aqueous alkali route.

questions.stem: Why must the halogenoalkane be primary for this route as taught?

options.explanation: No such hazard is the stated reason.

options.text: The taught substitution installs NH2 on a primary carbon to give a primary amine
options.explanation: The route as specified targets primary halogenoalkanes.

options.text: Secondary halogenoalkanes are too reactive to store
options.explanation: Storage stability is not the reason.

options.text: Ammonia cannot attack secondary carbons at all
options.explanation: The specification simply teaches the primary route.

questions.stem: Heating under pressure in the amine route serves to

options.explanation: Conditions are not catalysts.
No such conversion is part of the route.

options.text: Keep gaseous ammonia dissolved in the reacting ethanolic solution while warming the reaction
options.explanation: Pressure retains NH3 so the nucleophile stays available.

options.text: Raise the boiling point of the amine
options.explanation: The amine's properties are irrelevant.

questions.stem: State the conditions for the amine route.
questions.modelAnswer: Excess ethanolic ammonia, heated under pressure, with a primary halogenoalkane.

questions.stem: Name the organic product class and one example.
questions.modelAnswer: Primary amine; for example ethylamine from bromoethane.

questions.stem: Explain why the amine product could cause further substitution if ammonia were not in excess.
questions.modelAnswer: The amine's nitrogen still carries a lone pair, making it a nucleophile able to attack remaining halogenoalkane; excess ammonia out-competes it.

questions.stem: 1-bromopropane reacts with excess ethanolic ammonia under pressure. Name the product and state its carbon count.
questions.modelAnswer: Propylamine (a primary amine) with three carbons - the substitution conserves the chain length.

questions.stem: The conditions for the alkene route are

options.explanation: Aqueous conditions give substitution to the alcohol.
That gives the nitrile substitution.
Water hydrolyses too slowly and stays on the substitution track.
Ethanol solvent plus heat selects the elimination pathway.

questions.stem: In the elimination, the C-X bond breaks

options.text: Heterolytically, both electrons leaving with the halogen as X-
options.explanation: The pair departs with the electronegative halogen.

options.text: Homolytically, one electron to carbon and one to halogen
options.explanation: No radicals form in this route.

options.text: Not at all, as X- stays bonded
options.explanation: The halogen leaves as an ion.
Hydroxide takes hydrogen, not the C-X electrons.

questions.stem: Bromoethane heated with ethanolic NaOH gives

options.explanation: No ammonia is present.
The elimination installs the double bond on the two-carbon chain.
That is the aqueous route's product.
No cyanide is present.

questions.stem: The role of hydroxide in the elimination route is best described as

options.explanation: Ethanol is the solvent.
Hydroxide is consumed to water.

options.text: A base removing hydrogen so the double bond can form
options.explanation: The base's proton-abstraction role, not its nucleophilic one, dominates in ethanol.
That is the aqueous-route role.

questions.stem: Why does changing the solvent from water to ethanol flip substitution into elimination?

options.text: Ethanol reacts directly with the halogenoalkane
options.explanation: Ethanol is the solvent, not a reactant here.
Water supports substitution readily.

options.text: The halogen behaves differently in ethanol
options.explanation: The substrate is unchanged; the pathway balance shifts.

options.text: Solvation and conditions change the balance of pathways, favouring H removal over lone-pair attack
options.explanation: The medium tunes which role of OH- wins.

questions.stem: State the products when a halogenoalkane undergoes ethanolic elimination.
questions.modelAnswer: An alkene plus halide ion (X-) - the C-X bond breaks heterolytically.

questions.stem: State the elimination product from bromoethane.
questions.modelAnswer: Ethene, the two-carbon alkene carrying the new double bond.

questions.stem: Explain why heating is required for the elimination route.
questions.modelAnswer: Elimination has a higher energetic demand than substitution, so sustained heating under the ethanolic conditions drives the pathway.

questions.stem: Predict the product of 2-bromopropane with hot ethanolic NaOH and state what happens to the C-Br bond.
questions.modelAnswer: Propene forms; the C-Br bond breaks heterolytically, the electron pair leaving with bromide while the freed electrons build the C=C.
